demographics: No sex predilection, though attacks may be more frequent in women after puberty
Symptoms usually begin in childhood or adolescence and continue lifelong

risk_factors.text: Known C1 inhibitor deficiency or dysfunction

family_history: Hereditary angioedema in a parent or sibling
Unexplained recurrent swelling or abdominal attacks in relatives
Sudden death from airway swelling in a relative
exposures: Triggers include trauma, dental procedures, surgery, infections, emotional stress, and hormonal changes such as menstruation or pregnancy

chief_complaints.text: My hands and feet swell up
My stomach hurts so bad I can't stand up
My lips and face puff up
It feels like my throat is closing

hpi.onset: Sudden, over minutes to a few hours, often without warning
hpi.progression: Swelling builds over hours, peaks, then slowly resolves over days; attacks recur unpredictably
hpi.location: Can affect the face, lips, tongue, throat, hands, feet, genitals, or the gastrointestinal tract
hpi.radiation: Abdominal pain may be diffuse or crampy without radiation
hpi.quality: Non-pitting, non-itchy swelling; abdominal pain is crampy and colicky
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; airway involvement can be life-threatening
hpi.timing: Episodic, with symptom-free intervals between attacks
relieving: C1 inhibitor concentrate or other acute therapy
pertinent_negatives: Recent new medication or food exposure

positives.text: Swelling of the lips or tongue

argues_against: Inflammatory bowel disease or surgical abdomen

positives.text: Non-pitting swelling of the hands or feet

atypical.how_it_differs: Attacks may be milder or present as colicky abdominal pain and vomiting without obvious swelling; parents may report unexplained irritability.
Attacks may be less frequent but can still be severe; comorbid conditions can mimic or mask abdominal attacks.
Attack frequency may increase, especially in the second and third trimesters; swelling can be mistaken for normal pregnancy edema.

general.mild: Well-appearing, comfortable between attacks; during a mild attack, localized non-pitting swelling without distress
general.moderate: Uncomfortable, guarding the swollen area or abdomen, but not toxic; speaking normally
general.severe: Distressed, diaphoretic, sitting upright if the airway is involved; may have audible voice change or abdominal rigidity from pain
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, anxious, tripoding, unable to speak or swallow, with audible stridor or drooling; may be lethargic from hypoxia

labs.caveat: Usually normal or only mildly elevated; a marked rise points away from hereditary angioedema and toward an infectious or inflammatory cause.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging and because pregnancy affects attack frequency and treatment.

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Abdominal attack when another cause of acute abdomen must be excluded

findings.text: Free fluid in the abdomen or pelvis
Dilated, fluid-filled bowel loops from ileus
No obstruction, no free air, and no abscess

imaging.preferred_when: Children and pregnancy when another cause of abdominal pain must be excluded

findings.text: Free fluid in the abdomen or pelvis

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected deep neck infection or abscess when the airway is threatened

findings.text: Soft tissue swelling of the tongue, pharynx, or larynx without a discrete fluid collection
Usually normal; no infiltrate, pneumothorax, or mediastinal widening

initial.why: Best screening test; low between attacks strongly suggests hereditary angioedema
Looks for infection or another cause of abdominal pain
Assesses hydration and electrolytes during vomiting or poor intake
Rules out pregnancy before imaging and guides treatment

initial.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
initial.why: Excludes surgical and infectious causes of acute abdomen
initial.only_if: abdominal attack with severe pain or peritoneal concern

confirmatory.why: Low functional C1 inhibitor confirms the diagnosis in both type 1 and type 2
Distinguishes type 1 (low) from type 2 (normal or high)
Low C1q points to acquired rather than hereditary C1 inhibitor deficiency

supporting.why: A marked rise argues against hereditary angioedema and toward infection or inflammation

supporting.only_if: child or pregnant patient with abdominal pain

supporting.why: Looks for a deep neck infection or abscess
supporting.only_if: airway swelling with concern for abscess or epiglottitis

not_indicated.why: No role in angioedema or abdominal pain
Not needed unless the pain is epigastric and pancreatitis is suspected

decision_points: Draw complement studies when the patient is not in an acute attack if possible; acute attacks can lower C1 inhibitor levels transiently
Low C4 with low functional C1 inhibitor confirms hereditary angioedema; low C1q suggests the acquired form
Airway involvement is an emergency: secure the airway and give acute therapy without waiting for lab results
Pregnancy test before CT in anyone who could be pregnant
Avoid ACE inhibitors and estrogen-containing contraceptives in confirmed hereditary angioedema

criteria.name: Clinical and laboratory diagnosis of hereditary angioedema
criteria.summary: Recurrent non-urticarial, non-pitting swelling of the skin, gastrointestinal tract, or upper airway, often with a family history, plus low C4 and low functional C1 inhibitor. Type 1 also has low antigenic C1 inhibitor; type 2 has normal or high antigenic C1 inhibitor. Low C1q suggests the acquired form instead.

differential.name: Anaphylaxis and allergic angioedema
differential.why_considered: Acute swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or airway is the classic presentation of both, and both can be life-threatening.
differential.trigger: Swelling with urticaria, wheezing, hypotension, or a clear trigger such as a new food, drug, or sting

history: Onset within minutes of an exposure
Itchy hives or welts accompanying the swelling
Wheezing, chest tightness, or lightheadedness
Prior similar reactions to a specific allergen
No family history of recurrent swelling
exam: Swelling that is soft and pitting rather than firm
labs: Normal C4 and C1 inhibitor levels
Elevated serum tryptase in some cases
imaging: Chest x-ray usually normal; no role in diagnosis

differential.name: Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency
differential.why_considered: Presents with the same recurrent non-urticarial angioedema and abdominal attacks as hereditary angioedema but is not inherited.
differential.trigger: Adult onset of angioedema with no family history, especially with an underlying lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disorder

history: Onset in adulthood rather than childhood
No family history of angioedema
Associated lymphoproliferative disease, monoclonal gammopathy, or autoimmune disease
exam: Findings of an underlying disorder such as lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, or signs of autoimmune disease
labs: Low C4 and low functional C1 inhibitor
Low C1q, which is typically normal in hereditary angioedema
imaging: CT or ultrasound showing lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, or a mass suggesting an underlying malignancy

differential.name: ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema
differential.why_considered: A common cause of recurrent non-urticarial angioedema, particularly of the lips, tongue, and face, and can cause airway compromise.
differential.trigger: Angioedema in a patient taking an ACE inhibitor, with no childhood history or family history

history: Current or recent ACE inhibitor use
Onset after starting the medication
No childhood or family history of swelling
No abdominal attacks
exam: Swelling of the lips, tongue, or face without urticaria
labs: Normal C4 and C1 inhibitor levels

differential.name: Acute abdomen from a surgical cause (appendicitis, bowel obstruction)
differential.why_considered: Hereditary angioedema abdominal attacks cause severe crampy pain, vomiting, and distension that mimic a surgical abdomen.
differential.trigger: Localized tenderness with rebound or guarding, fever, or a rigid abdomen

history: Pain that migrates and localizes rather than being diffuse and colicky
Fever and anorexia
No prior episodes of self-limited swelling
No family history of angioedema
exam: Localized tenderness with rebound or involuntary guarding
Bowel sounds that are high-pitched or absent
labs: Normal C4 and C1 inhibitor levels
imaging: CT showing appendiceal inflammation, obstruction, free air, or an abscess

differential.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
differential.why_considered: Recurrent abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea can resemble hereditary angioedema abdominal attacks.

history: Chronic diarrhea, sometimes bloody
Weight loss and fatigue over weeks to months
Symptoms are continuous rather than episodic with complete resolution
exam: Weight loss, pallor, or perianal disease
Abdominal tenderness that is more localized
labs: Normal C4 and C1 inhibitor levels
imaging: Bowel wall thickening, skip lesions, or fistulas on CT or MRI enterography

differential.name: Epiglottitis and deep neck infection
differential.why_considered: Presents with throat pain, difficulty swallowing, voice change, and airway compromise that can mimic laryngeal angioedema.
differential.trigger: Fever, severe sore throat, drooling, and muffled voice with rapid progression

history: Fever and severe sore throat
Rapid onset over hours with systemic symptoms
No recurrent self-limited swelling episodes
imaging: Lateral neck x-ray or CT showing an enlarged epiglottis or a rim-enhancing abscess

differential.name: Nephrotic syndrome
differential.why_considered: Causes generalized non-pitting edema that can be mistaken for peripheral angioedema.

history: Gradual, persistent swelling rather than episodic attacks
Frothy urine
No family history of angioedema
labs: Normal C4 and C1 inhibitor levels
imaging: Renal ultrasound may show enlarged kidneys

severity.mild: Localized non-pitting swelling of an extremity or the face without airway or abdominal involvement; patient is comfortable and able to eat, drink, and speak normally.
severity.moderate: Swelling of the face, lips, or tongue with discomfort, or a significant abdominal attack with crampy pain, nausea, and vomiting; no airway compromise and able to swallow.
severity.severe: Laryngeal or tongue swelling with voice change, difficulty swallowing, or dyspnea, or a severe abdominal attack with distension and inability to tolerate oral intake; airway is threatened but still patent.
severity.critical: Airway obstruction with stridor, inability to speak or swallow, drooling, hypoxia, or hypotension; requires immediate airway management and acute therapy.

red_flags.finding: Stridor, hoarseness, or a muffled voice
red_flags.meaning: Laryngeal edema with impending airway obstruction; secure the airway and give acute therapy immediately

red_flags.finding: Difficulty swallowing, drooling, or inability to handle secretions
red_flags.meaning: Severe pharyngeal or laryngeal swelling; high risk of complete airway obstruction
Airway compromise or respiratory failure; emergency intervention needed

red_flags.finding: Swelling of the tongue or floor of the mouth
red_flags.meaning: Rapidly progressive airway threat; do not wait for imaging or labs

red_flags.finding: Severe abdominal pain with distension, vomiting, and hypotension
red_flags.meaning: Severe intestinal wall edema with hypovolemia from third-spacing; needs IV fluids and acute therapy
Hypovolemia from fluid shifts or a severe attack; assess for shock

complications.name: Hypovolemia and shock from intestinal fluid shifts
Unnecessary abdominal surgery for a presumed surgical abdomen
clues: Severe abdominal pain with vomiting and distension

complications.name: Opioid or fluid overload from inappropriate treatment

special_populations.differences: Attacks may present as colicky abdominal pain and vomiting without obvious swelling; parents may report unexplained irritability. Diagnosis is often delayed, and attacks may become more frequent after puberty.
Attacks may be less frequent but can still be severe; comorbid conditions can mimic or mask abdominal attacks, and polypharmacy increases the risk of ACE inhibitor use.

Attack frequency may increase, especially in the second and third trimesters; swelling can be mistaken for normal pregnancy edema. Treatment is adjusted because some agents are preferred over others, and attacks can complicate labor and delivery.

key_questions.question: What exactly swells during an attack — your face, lips, tongue, throat, hands, feet, or genitals?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent swelling of the skin, upper airway, or genitals; airway involvement is the dangerous site

key_questions.question: Does the swelling itch, and do you get hives or welts with it?
key_questions.looking_for: Non-itchy, non-pitting swelling without urticaria; itching or hives point to allergic angioedema

key_questions.question: How fast does the swelling come on, and how long does an attack last?
key_questions.looking_for: Builds over minutes to hours and resolves over 2–5 days; allergic reactions peak within minutes to an hour

key_questions.question: Have you had attacks of severe crampy belly pain with vomiting or diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent self-limited abdominal attacks that resolve without surgery

key_questions.question: Has anything brought on the attacks — trauma, dental work, surgery, stress, infections, or your period?
key_questions.looking_for: Recognized triggers such as trauma, dental procedures, stress, menstruation, or hormonal change

key_questions.question: Do antihistamines, steroids, or epinephrine help the swelling?
key_questions.looking_for: Little or no response; a clear response suggests allergic or histaminergic angioedema

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had recurrent swelling, unexplained abdominal attacks, or died suddenly from throat swelling?
key_questions.looking_for: Autosomal dominant family history of angioedema or sudden airway death

key_questions.question: When did the attacks first start?
key_questions.looking_for: Childhood or adolescence onset; adult onset with no family history suggests the acquired form

key_questions.question: Are you taking any blood pressure medicine, especially an ACE inhibitor like lisinopril or enalapril?
key_questions.looking_for: ACE inhibitor use, which causes a look-alike angioedema and must be stopped

key_questions.question: Are you taking estrogen — birth control pills, patches, or hormone therapy?
key_questions.looking_for: Estrogen exposure, which can worsen or trigger attacks

key_questions.question: Have you ever had trouble breathing, a hoarse or muffled voice, or trouble swallowing during an attack?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior or current laryngeal edema, which is life-threatening

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy, which can change attack frequency and treatment choices

reasoning_points: Recurrent, episodic, non-pitting, non-itchy swelling of the skin, upper airway, or gastrointestinal tract
No urticaria or pruritus with attacks, and poor response to antihistamines, corticosteroids, or epinephrine
Recurrent self-limited abdominal attacks with crampy pain, vomiting, and diarrhea that resolve without surgery
Positive family history consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance, or known C1 inhibitor deficiency
Onset in childhood or adolescence with lifelong recurrent attacks
Low C4 on screening, with low functional C1 inhibitor confirming the diagnosis
Low antigenic C1 inhibitor distinguishes type 1 from type 2 (normal or high antigenic level)
Normal C1q supports the hereditary form rather than acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency
ACE inhibitor use and allergic or anaphylactic angioedema have been excluded
Airway involvement is recognized as an emergency and treated before labs return

easy: Young patient with recurrent non-itchy swelling of the face, lips, or hands since childhood
Clear family history of hereditary angioedema
Attacks do not respond to antihistamines or steroids
Low C4 and low functional C1 inhibitor on labs
medium: Patient presents with a severe abdominal attack and no visible swelling, mimicking a surgical abdomen
Adult with recurrent swelling but no known family history
Patient on an ACE inhibitor, so drug-induced angioedema must be sorted out first
Attacks triggered by dental work, stress, or menstruation
hard: Isolated laryngeal edema as the first presentation with no prior swelling history
Child with colicky abdominal pain and vomiting but no visible swelling
Pregnant patient whose swelling is attributed to normal pregnancy edema
Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency with low C1q and an underlying lymphoproliferative disorder
Complement studies drawn during an acute attack and interpreted incorrectly
